ap_calculus_bc-m01.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane so that its position at time $t$ is $\bigl(x(t),y(t)\bigr)$, where $x(t)=2 t^{2}$ and $y(t)=2\left(\dfrac{t^3}{3}-t\right)$. What is the total distance traveled by the particle from $t=0$ to $t=2$?

options.why: Finds the straight-line distance between the positions at $t=0$ and $t=2$ instead of the length of the path.
$x'(t)=4t$ and $y'(t)=2 t^{2} - 2$, so the speed is $\sqrt{(4t)^2+(2 t^{2} - 2)^2}=2 t^{2} + 2$. The distance is $\int_0^{2}\left(2 t^{2} + 2\right)dt=\frac{28}{3}$.
Integrates $(x')^2+(y')^2$ and forgets the square root of the speed.
Reports the speed at $t=2$ instead of integrating the speed.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Total distance for planar motion is the integral of speed; the speed here simplifies because the sum of squares is a perfect square
student_thinking: Write the speed sqrt((x')^2 + (y')^2)
Notice that the expression under the root is a perfect square and take the root
Integrate the speed from 0 to the final time

key_conditions.condition: distance traveled equals the integral of speed
key_conditions.evidence: the speed a(t^2+1) is positive, so no part of the path is retraced

verification.independent_path: scipy quad of hypot(x'(t), y'(t)) over [0, b] (independent of the perfect-square simplification)

ap_calculus_bc-m01.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane so that its position at time $t$ is $\bigl(x(t),y(t)\bigr)$, where $x(t)=t^{2}$ and $y(t)=\left(\dfrac{t^3}{3}-t\right)$. What is the total distance traveled by the particle from $t=0$ to $t=3$?

options.why: Finds the straight-line distance between the positions at $t=0$ and $t=3$ instead of the length of the path.
$x'(t)=2t$ and $y'(t)=t^{2} - 1$, so the speed is $\sqrt{(2t)^2+(t^{2} - 1)^2}=t^{2} + 1$. The distance is $\int_0^{3}\left(t^{2} + 1\right)dt=12$.
Reports the speed at $t=3$ instead of integrating the speed.

ap_calculus_bc-m02.stem: A curve in the $xy$-plane is defined by the parametric equations $x=\dfrac{t^3}{3}-4t$ and $y=t^{2}$. For which values of $t$ is the curve concave up?

options.why: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2t}{t^2-4}$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(dy/dx\right)}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{-2(t^2+4)}{(t^2-4)^3}$. This is positive exactly when $t^2-4<0$, that is, when $-2<t<2$.
Uses the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ (positive slope) instead of the sign of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$.

For $t>2$ the second derivative $-2(t^2+4)/(t^2-4)^3$ is negative, so the curve is concave down there; the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ changes nowhere on this interval, which is not the same as concave up.
Uses $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}=2>0$, which is the concavity of $y$ as a function of $t$, not the concavity of the curve.

blueprint.concept: Decide the concavity of a parametric curve from the sign of d2y/dx2 = (d/dt(dy/dx))/(dx/dt)

Differentiate dy/dx with respect to t and divide by dx/dt
Find where the result is positive, keeping the points with dx/dt = 0 out

key_conditions.condition: concave up means d2y/dx2 > 0 and d2y/dx2 is defined only where dx/dt is not 0
key_conditions.evidence: the curve has a vertical tangent where t = +-a

misconceptions.description: uses the second derivative with respect to t

options.why: Uses the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ (positive slope) instead of the sign of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$.
Uses $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}=6>0$, which is the concavity of $y$ as a function of $t$, not the concavity of the curve.

For $t>1$ the second derivative $-6(t^2+1)/(t^2-1)^3$ is negative, so the curve is concave down there; the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ changes nowhere on this interval, which is not the same as concave up.

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{6t}{t^2-1}$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(dy/dx\right)}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{-6(t^2+1)}{(t^2-1)^3}$. This is positive exactly when $t^2-1<0$, that is, when $-1<t<1$.

ap_calculus_bc-m03.stem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=4\cos t$ and $y=2\sin t$ for $0\le t\le 2\pi$. Which of the following is an equation in $x$ and $y$ whose graph is this curve?

options.why: Divides by the amplitudes $4$ and $2$ instead of their squares.
$\cos t=\dfrac{x}{4}$ and $\sin t=\dfrac{y}{2}$, so $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$ becomes $\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}=1$.
Swaps the two denominators, so the semi-axes lie along the wrong coordinate axes.
Uses a minus sign, which would give a hyperbola; $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$ gives a plus sign.

ap_calculus_bc-m04.stem: A curve is defined by $x=\cos t$ and $y=\cos 2t$ for $0\le t\le 2\pi$. At how many values of $t$ in this interval does the curve have a horizontal tangent line?

options.why: Counts the values of $t$ with $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}\ne0$ (vertical tangents).

$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\sin t$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-2\sin 2t=-4\sin t\cos t$, which is $0$ at $t=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ 2\pi$. Where $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ is also $0$, simplify $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4\cos t$ and read its value there. Exactly $2$ of the values of $t$ give slope $0$.
Counts every zero of $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ except the one at the endpoint $t=2\pi$.
Counts only the interior zeros of $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ and leaves out the endpoints $t=0$ and $t=2\pi$.

ap_calculus_bc-m05.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane with velocity vector $\vec v(t)=\left\langle 2 t^{2} - 2 t + 2,\ 2 t - 3\right\rangle$ for $0\le t\le 4$. At what time $t$ is the speed of the particle least?

options.why: The speed is $\sqrt{x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2}$. Using a calculator to minimize $x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2$ on $[0,4]$ gives $t=0.862$, and the speeds at the endpoints $t=0$ and $t=4$ are larger.
Reports the left endpoint, where the speed is not least.
Reports the time at which $y'(t)=0$, where the vertical component of velocity vanishes, not the time of least speed.

ap_calculus_bc-m07.stem: The polar curve $r=3\sin(2\theta)$ has several petals. What is the area of the region enclosed by one petal of the curve?

$r=0$ at $\theta=0$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and $r\ge0$ between them, so one petal has area $\dfrac12\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(3\sin(2\theta)\right)^2d\theta=\frac{9 \pi}{8}$.
Leaves out the factor $\dfrac12$ in the polar area formula.

ap_calculus_bc-m08.stem: Let $R$ be the region that lies inside the polar curve $r=4+4\cos\theta$ and outside the polar curve $r=4$. Which of the following gives the area of $R$?

options.why: Uses the limits $0$ and $\pi$; the curves meet where $\cos\theta=0$, at $\theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and the region lies on both sides of the $x$-axis.

The curves meet where $4+4\cos\theta=4$, that is $\cos\theta=0$, at $\theta=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Between those angles the cardioid is the outer curve, so the area is $\dfrac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\left[(r_{\text{outer}})^2-(r_{\text{inner}})^2\right]d\theta$.
Leaves out the factor $\dfrac12$ of the polar area formula.
Subtracts the radii instead of the squares of the radii.

ap_calculus_bc-m10.stem: The graph of the polar curve $r=6\cos\theta$ for $0\le\theta\le\pi$ is which of the following?

options.text: A circle with center $(0,3)$ and radius $3$.
options.why: Swaps the roles of cosine and sine, so the circle is centered on the wrong axis.

options.text: A circle with center $(3,0)$ and radius $3$.
options.why: Multiplying by $r$ gives $r^2=6\,r\cos\theta$, so $x^2+y^2=6x$. Completing the square gives $(x-3)^2+y^2=9$, a circle with center $(3,0)$ and radius $3$.

options.text: A circle with center $(0,0)$ and radius $6$.
options.why: Treats $r=6\cos\theta$ as if it had a constant radius, so the circle would be centered at the origin.

options.text: A circle with center $(3,0)$ and radius $6$.
options.why: Finds the correct center but uses the diameter $6$ as the radius.

options.text: A circle with center $(0,1)$ and radius $1$.
options.why: Multiplying by $r$ gives $r^2=2\,r\sin\theta$, so $x^2+y^2=2y$. Completing the square gives $x^2+(y-1)^2=1$, a circle with center $(0,1)$ and radius $1$.

options.text: A circle with center $(0,1)$ and radius $2$.
options.why: Finds the correct center but uses the diameter $2$ as the radius.

options.text: A circle with center $(0,0)$ and radius $2$.
options.why: Treats $r=2\sin\theta$ as if it had a constant radius, so the circle would be centered at the origin.

ap_calculus_bc-m11.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane so that its velocity vector at time $t$ is $\vec v(t)=\left\langle 5 - 2 t,\ 5 - 2 t^{2}\right\rangle$. Which of the following statements is true at time $t=1$?

options.text: The particle is moving to the right and upward, and its speed is decreasing.
options.why: $\vec v(1)=\langle 3,3\rangle$ and $\vec a(t)=\left\langle -2,\ - 4 t\right\rangle$, so $\vec a(1)=\langle -2,-4\rangle$. The components of $\vec v$ give the direction, and $\vec v\cdot\vec a=-6-12=-18$ is negative, so the speed is decreasing.

options.text: The particle is moving to the right and upward, and its speed is increasing.
options.why: Takes the wrong sign for the rate of change of speed: speed increases when $\vec v\cdot\vec a>0$, and here $\vec v\cdot\vec a=-18$.

options.text: The particle is moving to the left and upward, and its speed is decreasing.
options.why: Reads the horizontal direction from the sign of the $x$-component of acceleration ($-2$) instead of the $x$-component of velocity ($3$).

options.text: The particle is moving to the right and downward, and its speed is decreasing.
options.why: Reads the vertical direction from the sign of the $y$-component of acceleration ($-4$) instead of the $y$-component of velocity ($3$).

key_conditions.evidence: the velocity is not the zero vector at the given time

ap_calculus_bc-m11.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane so that its velocity vector at time $t$ is $\vec v(t)=\left\langle t - 3,\ t^{2} - 4\right\rangle$. Which of the following statements is true at time $t=1$?

options.text: The particle is moving to the right and downward, and its speed is decreasing.
options.why: Reads the horizontal direction from the sign of the $x$-component of acceleration ($1$) instead of the $x$-component of velocity ($-2$).

options.text: The particle is moving to the left and downward, and its speed is increasing.
options.why: Takes the wrong sign for the rate of change of speed: speed increases when $\vec v\cdot\vec a>0$, and here $\vec v\cdot\vec a=-8$.

options.text: The particle is moving to the left and downward, and its speed is decreasing.
options.why: $\vec v(1)=\langle -2,-3\rangle$ and $\vec a(t)=\left\langle 1,\ 2 t\right\rangle$, so $\vec a(1)=\langle 1,2\rangle$. The components of $\vec v$ give the direction, and $\vec v\cdot\vec a=-2-6=-8$ is negative, so the speed is decreasing.

options.text: The particle is moving to the left and upward, and its speed is decreasing.
options.why: Reads the vertical direction from the sign of the $y$-component of acceleration ($2$) instead of the $y$-component of velocity ($-3$).

ap_calculus_bc-m12.stem: The position of a particle moving in the $xy$-plane at time $t$ is $\vec r(t)=\left\langle 2 t^{2} + t,\ 2 t^{3}\right\rangle$. What is the average velocity vector of the particle over the time interval $1\le t\le 3$?

options.why: $\vec r(3)=\left\langle 21,\ 54\right\rangle$ and $\vec r(1)=\left\langle 3,\ 2\right\rangle$, so the average velocity is $\dfrac{\vec r(3)-\vec r(1)}{3-1}=\left\langle 9,\ 26\right\rangle$.
Averages the velocities at the endpoints, which is not the average velocity when a coordinate is cubic.
Reports the velocity at the midpoint $t=2$ instead of the average velocity; the second coordinate is cubic in $t$, so these differ.
Averages the endpoint positions instead of finding the change in position.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Average velocity vector is the change in the position vector divided by the elapsed time
student_thinking: Evaluate the position vector at both ends of the interval
Subtract and divide by the length of the interval

key_conditions.condition: average velocity over [a, b] = (r(b) - r(a))/(b - a)
key_conditions.evidence: definition for vector-valued functions

verification.independent_path: difference quotient of the numerically evaluated position components over the interval (independent of the sympy substitution)

ap_calculus_bc-m13.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane with velocity vector $\vec v(t)=\left\langle 4 t + 1,\ \dfrac{4}{t+1}\right\rangle$ for $t\ge 0$. At time $t=0$ the particle is at the point $(5,2)$. What is the position of the particle at time $t=2$?

options.why: Adds the initial position to the first coordinate only.
Evaluates the velocity vector at $t=2$ instead of integrating it.
Reverses the roles of the two initial coordinates.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Recover a position vector by integrating each component of the velocity vector and adding the initial position
student_thinking: Integrate the x-component and the y-component separately from 0 to the given time
Use an antiderivative of 1/(t+1) that is a logarithm
Add the initial position to each coordinate

key_conditions.condition: position equals initial position plus the integral of velocity, componentwise
key_conditions.evidence: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus applied to each coordinate

options.why: Uses $\dfrac{-1}{(t+1)^2}$ (the derivative) instead of $\ln|t+1|$ as the antiderivative of $\dfrac{1}{t+1}$ in the second coordinate.
